sources.title: Human History Map historical-basemap civilization index
sources.note: Exact repository records checked: xiongnu is circa 400 to 323 BCE; xiongnu-bc200 and southern-xiongnu are separate later ids. The early card is never aliased to either successor record.

sources.title: Human History Map world-500 BCE topology
sources.note: Decoded predecessor snapshot. The tested Mongolian-steppe points fall inside proto-altaic-pastoralists, a broad and problematic atlas umbrella rather than a verified ethnic border.

sources.title: Human History Map world-400 BCE topology
sources.note: Decoded exact feature: one Polygon, one ring, 17 positions, bbox 81.423814 to 132.342723°E and 38.961739 to 53.494313°N. Ulaanbaatar, Khangai, south Baikal and east Altai test inside; Ordos, Hohhot, Kashgar and Beijing do not.

sources.title: Human History Map world-323 BCE topology
sources.note: Decoded successor seam. The exact xiongnu id disappears and no replacement covers the tested Mongolian core, demonstrating an atlas coverage gap rather than a historical extinction.

sources.title: Human History Map world-200 BCE topology
sources.note: Decoded later feature: the distinct xiongnu-bc200 id appears as one 20-position polygon. It is the atlas handoff for the documented imperial confederation, not an alias of the early missing id.

sources.title: Human History Map world-100 CE topology
sources.note: Decoded late seam. The atlas uses the distinct southern-xiongnu id for a small one-ring feature in 100 to 200 CE, while its broad northern imperial record has ended.

sources.title: Bryan K. Miller, Xiongnu: The World’s First Nomadic Empire
sources.note: Oxford University Press scholarly monograph and chapter listing checked for the long arc from diverse eastern-steppe communities through imperial consolidation, mobile government, political economy, archaeology and contested afterlives.

sources.title: Encyclopaedia Iranica, Xiongnu
sources.note: Scholarly reference checked for the first Chinese textual mention in 318 BCE, fourth-century BCE mounted elites at expanding northern frontiers, empire chronology, towns, agriculture, exchange and the debated Xiongnu to Hun connection.

sources.title: The Origin of Xiongnu Archaeological Culture Based on Funeral Rites
sources.note: Mongolian Journal of Anthropology, Archaeology and Ethnology article. Early “xiongnuization” is traced cautiously through fourth to third-century BCE tombs retaining features of earlier slab-grave traditions; competing homeland theories remain unresolved.

sources.title: Early nomads of the Eastern Steppe and their tentative connections in the West
sources.note: Open Cambridge interdisciplinary review checked for the 209 to 161 BCE consolidation, mixed pastoral-agricultural economy, Chinese-source bias, uncertain homeland and language, later division, and limits of linking the Xiongnu to European Huns.

sources.title: Yale News, Mobile culture: an archaeologist sifts through Mongolia’s ancient past
sources.note: Interview with archaeologist William Honeychurch checked for state formation under Modu around the third century BCE, the distinct organization of mobile societies, regional survey methods and seasonal-habitation evidence.

sources.title: Chinese Text Project, Shiji chapter 110: Xiongnu liezhuan
sources.note: Digital primary text of Sima Qian’s transmitted classical-Chinese account. Used as an invaluable but external and politically situated Han-era source for names, titles, frontier events and the authentic written heading 匈奴列傳.

sources.title: Chelsea Hite, Mobile Subjects: Technologies of Power in the Xiongnu Empire
sources.note: University of Chicago dissertation checked for source criticism and the finding that no clear empirical evidence for a Xiongnu script survives; diplomatic letters known from texts were written in Chinese.

sources.title: The Nomad as State Builder: Historical Theory and Material Evidence from Mongolia
sources.note: Peer-reviewed Journal of World Prehistory synthesis checked for archaeological evidence of a late-first-millennium BCE Xiongnu polity and for the danger of forcing mobile political organization into sedentary-state models.

sources.title: Masters of the Steppe
sources.note: Oxford scholarly chapter abstract checked for early conquests, centralized imperial rule after Modu, ranks around a supreme chanyu and control of animals, people, grains and luxury resources.

sources.title: Genetic population structure of the Xiongnu Empire at imperial and local scales
sources.note: Open Science Advances study checked for extreme genetic diversity, frontier communities, high-status women, children and varied ancestry. Genetic ancestry is not treated as language, ethnicity or a political passport.

sources.title: Genetic relatedness, social status and cemetery organisation: the Xiongnu Tamir necropolis
sources.note: Open Antiquity article checked for spouses and young children, selective burial, lineage, status, adoption, female succession and the warning that one cemetery was organized by more than biological kinship.

sources.title: Local circulation of elites punctuated by transregional mobility enabled steppe political consolidation
sources.note: Open isotope study checked for local and nonlocal childhood signatures, livestock-based diets, seasonal winter grazing and likely pasture infrastructure. Its sampled cemeteries cannot describe every household.

sources.title: The Xiongnu settlements of Egiin Gol, Mongolia
sources.note: Antiquity research abstract checked for pastoralism, cultivation, ceramics and settlement hierarchy, correcting the stereotype that archaeology reveals only wandering camps and tombs.

sources.title: Economic Diversification Supported the Growth of Mongolia’s Nomadic Empires
sources.note: Open Scientific Reports isotope study checked for mixed economies combining dairy pastoralism with millet and other crops, variation between individuals and regions, and diversification as protection against environmental and political shocks.

sources.title: Dairy pastoralism sustained Eastern Eurasian Steppe populations for 5000 years
sources.note: Open Nature Ecology & Evolution study checked for milk-protein evidence, long eastern-steppe dairy traditions and neighboring written evidence for ruminant and horse-milk consumption by the Xiongnu period.

sources.title: The human environment of the Xiongnu Ivolga Fortress
sources.note: Peer-reviewed Quaternary International article checked for the Selenga-valley setting, 54 excavated dwellings, hundreds of household pits, cereals, fish, wild animals and domestic stock at the unusually well-preserved fortified settlement.

sources.title: The innovation of iron and the Xiongnu: a case study from Central Mongolia
sources.note: Asian Archaeology article checked for furnaces, tuyères, charcoal and increasing bloomery efficiency. The strongest evidence belongs to imperial centuries and is not projected wholesale onto 400 BCE.

sources.title: Technological traditions inferred from iron artefacts of the Xiongnu Empire in Mongolia
sources.note: Journal of Archaeological Science study checked for low-carbon iron, carburization, limited cast iron and a local bloomery tradition distinct from Han cast-iron production.

sources.title: Composite Bows from Uch-Kurbu in Kyrgyzstan
sources.note: Archaeology, Ethnology and Anthropology of Eurasia abstract checked for reconstructed Xiongnu to Xianbei-period composite bows with wood cores and horn plates. This later technical evidence does not specify the bow used by every early herder.

sources.title: Metropolitan Museum of Art, Belt Plaque with Fighting Horses
sources.note: Museum collection record checked for a bronze Xiongnu-culture belt plaque from northwest China dated to the second to first century BCE. Used as one object, not a universal costume.

sources.title: Clothes from the Xiongnu Wardrobe, based on Noin-Ula finds
sources.note: Peer-reviewed clothing study checked for elite silk, wool, fur, felt, birch-bark soles, locally assembled caftans and leggings, and its explicit warning that an entire Xiongnu wardrobe cannot yet be reconstructed.

sources.title: Noyon Uul archaeological textiles and felt-making heritage
sources.note: Acta Via Serica article checked for embroidered felt blankets, carpets, rugs, curtain-like pieces and dwelling covers recovered from elite burials, plus continuity of felt-working traditions. Funerary textiles are not ordinary-house inventories.

sources.title: UNESCO, Cemetery Complexes of the Xiongnu Nobility
sources.note: World Heritage record checked for imperial dates, Steppe Route contacts, deep tomb engineering, satellite graves, paired-stone sacrificial structures, horse tack, chariots, tools and food offerings; UNESCO notes that much remains unknown.

sources.title: Stone lines and burnt bones: ritual elaborations in Xiongnu mortuary arenas
sources.note: Open Antiquity study checked for distinct mortuary events, sheep and cattle offerings, meat portions, animal extremities, ritual fires and competitive expenditure around elite cemeteries.

sources.title: Dental Caries Prevalence in Xiongnu Population from Mongolia
sources.note: Mongolian Journal study checked: 110 skulls and 1,394 teeth, 17.3 percent of examined individuals with caries, regional and age variation, and a cautious inference of increased carbohydrate consumption.

sources.title: Hou Hanshu, volume 89: Treatise on the Southern Xiongnu
sources.note: Bilingual transmitted primary text checked for later Southern Xiongnu assemblies, sacrifices and horse and camel racing for enjoyment. This is evidence for a later branch, not proof of children’s games in 400 BCE.

sources.title: ICOMOS evaluation, Cemetery Complexes of the Xiongnu Nobility
sources.note: Official 2026 evaluation checked for the low archaeological visibility of mobile life, known settlements and production sites, tomb research history, and long-distance goods including Chinese lacquer and Mediterranean glass.

sources.title: Technology and chronology of metal from Tamiryn Ulaan Khoshuu
sources.note: Archaeometry study checked for copper-tin-lead ornaments, cast-iron household objects, radiocarbon dates reaching the fourth century BCE and early regionally connected Xiongnu-style material culture.

sources.title: Settled Population in the Xiongnu Empire: Ivolga fortress example
sources.note: Peer-reviewed archaeology abstract checked for farmers and craftspeople, possible captives or semi-vassals, tribute relations, adult and child graves, and marked inequality at Ivolga. Social labels remain interpretations, not names spoken by residents.

sources.title: Max Planck Institute, Genetic History of Mongolia
sources.note: Research-institute summary checked for distinct Bronze and Iron Age regional gene pools and their mixture during Xiongnu formation. Population genetics is used only for ancestry and mobility, never to assign a language.

sources.title: Health and nutritional status of the Xiongnu population
sources.note: Open paleopathology study page checked for skeletal approaches to nutrition and for its finding of similar male and female access to food in its sample. It does not reveal particular medicines or healers.

sources.title: Social Complexity and Political Capitals in Ancient Eurasia
sources.note: Oxford Handbook chapter checked for Ivolga agriculture, pastoralism and metalwork, and for dispersed, low-density, itinerant habitation across much of the Xiongnu landscape rather than one mandatory capital model.

scopeNotes: New text needs independent review; earlier hashes do not certify it.
Map endpoints are not historical founding or extinction dates.
Agent researched a disjoint batch; integration and structural checks are not independent historical certification.
Imported border coordinates remain unchanged. Historical events and map coverage are distinguished in prose; see batchIdentityNotes for conflicts.

proposedOverrides.summary: Early steppe coalitions became the Xiongnu empire around 209 BCE; archaeology reveals mobile work, mixed foodways, families, crafts and wide exchange while the atlas dates remain approximate.

batchIdentityNotes: Exact target xiongnu is indexed circa 400 to 323 BCE and has no tracked card or override before integration.
Its only exact feature is world-bc400: one Polygon, one ring, 17 positions, bbox 81.423814 to 132.342723 E and 38.961739 to 53.494313 N.

The predecessor layer uses proto-altaic-pastoralists; the 323 BCE layer leaves the tested Mongolian core uncovered. These are atlas categorization changes and gaps, not verified ethnic or political seams.

The first explicit textual mention commonly cited is 318 BCE and Modu’s imperial consolidation is around 209 BCE. The early card uses the map interval as a cautious origins frame, not a founding claim.
xiongnu-bc200 and southern-xiongnu are separate existing/missing atlas records. No appliesTo alias or shared-card substitution is used.
Geometry and point tests are display evidence only and do not establish allegiance, seasonal range, language, ancestry or modern territorial claims.
